opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the big lesson for me was that weather turned out to be almost the perfect stress test for the whole neural operator idea. When we started on FourCastNet, a lot of people in the weather community were skeptical, and honestly for good reason. Numerical weather prediction is one of the great triumphs of scientific computing. Decades of physics, careful numerics, huge supercomputers. The idea that a data-driven model could compete seemed far-fetched.

What we learned is that if you design the architecture around the structure of the problem, you can get there. Weather is fundamentally about continuous fields evolving on the sphere, governed by PDEs. A standard vision model treats it like an image at a fixed resolution, and that breaks down. Neural operators instead learn a mapping between function spaces. You're learning the solution operator itself, not just a pixel-to-pixel mapping. The Fourier neural operator does a lot of its work in the spectral domain, which is natural for these global, multi-scale dynamics.

Then we hit a real problem: the sphere. The plain FFT assumes a flat, periodic domain, and when you roll out the forecast autoregressively for weeks you get artifacts, especially near the poles, and things blow up. That pushed us to the spherical Fourier neural operator, using spherical harmonics so the model respects the geometry. That gave us stable rollouts over much longer horizons. So the lesson there was that getting the inductive bias right matters a lot more than just scaling the model.

The second big lesson was about speed and what it unlocks. Once you have a model that's orders of magnitude faster than traditional numerical solvers, you aren't just making one forecast cheaper. You can run huge ensembles, thousands of members, on a handful of GPUs. That changes what's possible for things like extreme events and tail risks. Heat waves and hurricanes are the rare events you care most about, and you need very large ensembles to characterize them properly.

The third lesson was that data-driven doesn't mean physics-free. The models were trained on reanalysis data like ERA5, which is itself the product of physics-based data assimilation. And we've been folding in physical constraints and resolution invariance so you can train at one resolution and evaluate at another. That's where operators really shine compared to standard neural nets.

And frankly, there was a cultural lesson too. Showing that this works on something as high-stakes and well-benchmarked as weather got people to take AI for science seriously. Since then you've seen many groups and operational centers build on this, and now the conversation has moved from "can AI do weather?" to "how do we make it trustworthy, calibrated, and useful for decisions." To me that's the most exciting outcome. Weather was the proof point, and the same ideas carry over to climate, fluid dynamics, materials, and many other scientific domains.

r001.rationale: The response says a data-driven model could “compete” and that the approach can work, but it does not clearly state that forecast accuracy nearly matched traditional weather models.

r002.rationale: The response says the model was “orders of magnitude faster,” but does not state that it was tens of thousands of times faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Weather was really the first big test case for us, and honestly it taught me more than any benchmark could. The reason we picked weather is that it's the one domain where you have decades of high-quality, consistent observational data, you have very mature numerical models to compare against, and the stakes are obvious to everyone. So if neural operators were going to fail, it would fail visibly, and if they worked, people would care.

The first lesson was that resolution independence actually matters in practice, not just as a nice mathematical property. Traditional neural networks are tied to the grid you train them on. A neural operator learns the mapping between function spaces, so you can train at one resolution and evaluate at another, and that turned out to be essential because the real atmosphere isn't a fixed grid. With FourCastNet we were working at roughly a quarter degree globally, and the fact that we could reason about the problem in Fourier space, where the dynamics are naturally expressed, made the model both faster and more physically sensible.

The second lesson was about speed, and how speed changes what you can even ask. Numerical weather prediction is incredibly expensive. You run it on a supercomputer, you get maybe fifty ensemble members, and that's your uncertainty estimate. When the learned model is tens of thousands of times faster, you can suddenly run thousands of ensemble members. That isn't just a cheaper version of the same thing. It changes the science, because now you can actually characterize the probability of extreme events, hurricanes, atmospheric rivers, heat waves, in a way that wasn't computationally possible before.

The third lesson, and this is the humbling one, was about the gap between a good benchmark number and a trustworthy forecast. Early on we'd see beautiful metrics on things like 500 hectopascal geopotential height, and then you'd look at the precipitation and it would be smeared out. The models want to regress toward the mean, because that's what minimizes the loss. So we had to think hard about spectral fidelity, about not losing the small scales, and about how you evaluate extremes specifically rather than averages. That pushed us toward things like spherical harmonics, so the model respects the geometry of the globe, and toward longer rollout stability, because a model that's great at six hours and blows up at ten days isn't useful.

And then the broader lesson for me was that this wasn't really about weather. Weather was the proof point that you can learn the solution operator of a complex PDE system from data and have it generalize. Once that landed, the same ideas carried over to carbon capture, to plasma in fusion reactors, to fluid dynamics in design. The weather work gave us the confidence and the community credibility to say neural operators are a general tool for scientific computing, not a trick that happens to work on one dataset.

r001.rationale: The response mentions strong benchmark metrics but does not state that forecast accuracy nearly matched traditional weather models.

r002.rationale: It says the learned model is “tens of thousands of times faster” than numerical weather prediction.

astra-6.text:
One of the biggest lessons was that you need to learn the dynamics, not just fit the next snapshot. With neural operators, we learn mappings between functions—in this case, from one atmospheric state to the next. That gives us a way to model a system that evolves over space and time.

But a good one-step prediction doesn’t automatically give you a good forecast. When you feed predictions back into the model, errors can accumulate. So you have to evaluate the whole rollout: Does it remain stable? Does it capture important structures? How does it behave on extreme events, rather than just on average conditions?

The speed also changes what you can do. You can run many forecasts to explore uncertainty. For me, that’s a particularly exciting direction: using fast models to understand the range of possible outcomes, while working closely with domain scientists to make sure we’re measuring what matters.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the biggest lessons was that you have to think beyond one-step prediction. A model can look very accurate at predicting the next weather state, but when you repeatedly feed its predictions back in, small errors can accumulate. So the question becomes: Has it learned enough of the underlying dynamics to produce a useful forecast over time?

Neural operators give us a way to learn mappings between fields—an atmospheric state evolving into another atmospheric state—rather than treating everything as a fixed-dimensional vector. That’s a very natural fit for weather. You need to capture both large-scale circulation and smaller-scale structure, and how they interact.

But speed alone isn’t enough. You also need to understand extremes, uncertainty, and where the model fails. The exciting possibility is to use that speed to generate many forecasts and explore a range of outcomes. That makes the problem much more than simply replacing a numerical simulator with a faster prediction.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can be accurate at next-state prediction, but it does not say neural operators nearly matched traditional weather models in forecasting accuracy.
